items.question: Which option best defines the legal concept of litigation?
items.correct: The formal process by which a dispute is carried through the courts to a binding decision
distractors: An informal agreement reached privately between two disputing parties outside of a courtroom
The process of drafting a new legislative bill to be presented to the national assembly
A preliminary investigation conducted by law enforcement officers prior to a formal arrest
items.note: Litigation is the court process itself, not the dispute and not the settlement.
items.example: The firm has been in litigation with its former supplier for eighteen months.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Culpable'.
items.correct: Guilty
distractors: Involved
Accused
Reckless
items.note: Culpable means deserving blame; it is stronger than merely 'involved'.
items.example: The inquiry found the contractor culpable for the collapse of the walkway.

items.question: What does an indictment formally represent?
items.correct: A formal written charge accusing a named person of a serious criminal offence
distractors: The final decision of guilt delivered by a jury at the close of a criminal trial
A written statement of the punishment imposed on a defendant after conviction
An official pardon granted to a prisoner by the head of state or a governor
items.note: An indictment starts a prosecution; it is an accusation, never a finding of guilt.
items.example: The grand jury returned an indictment on three counts of fraud.

items.question: The ________ filed the claim, alleging that the company had breached the terms of the contract.
items.correct: plaintiff
distractors: solicitor
witness
registrar
items.note: The plaintiff brings the case; the defendant answers it.
items.example: The plaintiff is seeking damages of two million baht.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Statute'.
items.correct: Law
distractors: Custom
Guideline
Ruling
items.note: A statute is written law passed by a legislature, not custom or case law.
items.example: The practice is prohibited under a statute passed last year.

items.question: What is an injunction in legal practice?
items.correct: An order of a court requiring a party to do something or to stop doing something
distractors: A financial penalty imposed on a company for repeatedly violating a regulatory requirement
A formal request asking a higher court to review the decision of a lower court
A confidential agreement in which neither party admits any legal responsibility
items.note: An injunction compels behaviour; it is an order, not a payment or an appeal.
items.example: The union obtained an injunction halting the demolition work.

items.question: The ruling set an important ________ that lower courts will be obliged to follow.
items.correct: precedent
distractors: custom
deadline
exception
items.note: A precedent is an earlier decision that binds or guides later ones.
items.example: There is no precedent for compensation on this scale.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Liable'.
items.correct: Exempt
distractors: Insured
Solvent
Compliant
items.note: Liable means legally responsible; exempt means freed from that responsibility.
items.example: Directors may be personally liable for the debts of the company.

items.question: What does it mean to acquit a defendant?
items.correct: To declare formally at the end of a trial that the person is not guilty as charged
distractors: To release a convicted prisoner early on condition of continued good behaviour
To reduce a sentence in recognition of the defendant's cooperation with investigators
To postpone a trial until further evidence has been gathered by the prosecution
items.note: An acquittal ends the charge; it is not parole and not a delay.
items.example: The jury acquitted her after four hours of deliberation.

items.question: What is a deposition?
items.correct: Testimony given on oath outside the courtroom and recorded before a trial begins
distractors: The written judgment issued by a court once all arguments have finally been heard
A sworn statement written by a party and signed in the presence of a notary
The opening speech delivered by counsel at the beginning of a criminal trial
items.note: A deposition is spoken testimony under oath, recorded before trial.
items.example: Counsel spent two days taking the engineer's deposition.

items.question: The tribunal declined the case on the ground that it fell outside its ________.
items.correct: jurisdiction
distractors: expertise
budget
premises
items.note: Jurisdiction is the legal power to hear a matter, defined by subject and territory.
items.example: Offshore contracts often fall under a foreign jurisdiction.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Mitigate' in a legal context.
items.correct: Lessen
distractors: Excuse
Deny
Delay
items.note: To mitigate is to reduce severity; it is not to excuse or to deny.
items.example: Her cooperation with the police was treated as a strong mitigating factor.

items.question: What is an affidavit?
items.correct: A written statement of fact which its maker swears to be true and may use as evidence
distractors: An oral account given by a witness while under examination in open court proceedings
A summary of legal arguments prepared by counsel and submitted before a hearing begins
A formal notice ordering a person to appear before a court on a specified date
items.note: An affidavit is written and sworn; testimony in court is spoken.
items.example: He filed an affidavit setting out the sequence of events.

items.question: What does arbitration involve?
items.correct: Settling a dispute by referring it to a neutral third party whose decision the parties accept
distractors: A structured negotiation in which the parties themselves reach a compromise without any outsider
A public hearing before a panel of elected judges in the commercial division of the court
An investigation carried out by a government regulator into the conduct of an industry
items.note: An arbitrator decides; a mediator only helps the parties decide for themselves.
items.example: The contract requires arbitration in Singapore rather than litigation.

items.question: Failing to deliver the goods on the agreed date constitutes a ________ of contract.
items.correct: breach
distractors: variation
renewal
summary
items.note: A breach is a failure to keep a legal obligation.
items.example: The late payment was a clear breach of the lease.

items.question: In family law, what does custody refer to?
items.correct: The legal right to care for a child and to make decisions on the child's behalf
distractors: The financial support one parent is ordered to pay the other after a separation
The right of a parent to spend arranged periods of time with a child each month
The formal process by which an adult becomes the legal parent of another person's child
items.note: Custody is decision-making care; visitation and maintenance are separate rights.
items.example: The court granted joint custody to both parents.

items.question: What does defamation mean in law?
items.correct: Harming another person's reputation by making or publishing a false statement
distractors: Publishing private information about a person without obtaining their prior consent
Making an offensive remark directed at a person during a heated public argument
Using another person's name or image commercially without paying any compensation
items.note: Defamation needs falsity and reputational harm; true statements are not defamatory.
items.example: The newspaper faces a defamation claim over the allegations.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Negligence'.
items.correct: Diligence
distractors: Malice
Ignorance
Immunity
items.note: Negligence is failure to take reasonable care; diligence is its opposite, not intent.
items.example: The hospital denied any negligence in the patient's treatment.

items.question: The court issued a ________ compelling the accountant to produce the ledgers.
items.correct: subpoena
distractors: warrant
verdict
receipt
items.note: A subpoena compels attendance or the production of documents.
items.example: Ignoring a subpoena can amount to contempt of court.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Tenable' when describing an argument.
items.correct: Defensible
distractors: Persuasive
Irrefutable
Popular
items.note: A tenable argument can be defended; it is not necessarily proven or popular.
items.example: That reading of the clause is simply not tenable.

items.question: What is a verdict?
items.correct: The decision reached by a jury or by a judge on the disputed facts at a trial's end
distractors: The punishment that a judge imposes once guilt has been established in a criminal trial
The formal accusation read aloud to the defendant at the opening of the proceedings
The written explanation of the legal reasoning behind a decision of an appeal court
items.note: Verdict decides guilt or liability; the sentence comes afterwards.
items.example: The jury reached a unanimous verdict in under an hour.

items.question: What is a waiver?
items.correct: The deliberate and voluntary surrender of a legal right that a person would hold
distractors: A temporary suspension of a rule granted by a regulator for a limited period of time
A written promise to compensate another party for any losses they may later suffer
A formal objection raised against the admissibility of evidence during a hearing
items.note: A waiver surrenders a right; a suspension merely pauses an obligation.
items.example: Signing the waiver does not remove the operator's duty of care.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Adjudicate'.
items.correct: Judge
distractors: Mediate
Advocate
Investigate
items.note: To adjudicate is to decide formally, not to advocate or investigate.
items.example: The panel will adjudicate the dispute within thirty days.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Coercion'.
items.correct: Consent
distractors: Compliance
Encouragement
Authority
items.note: Coercion removes free choice; consent is choice freely given.
items.example: The confession was excluded because it was obtained by coercion.

items.question: What does it mean to exonerate someone?
items.correct: To clear a person completely of the blame or accusation previously made against them
distractors: To reduce the penalty imposed on them in recognition of mitigating personal circumstances
To grant them official forgiveness for an offence of which they were properly convicted
To transfer responsibility for their conduct onto the organisation that employed them
items.note: Exoneration removes blame; a pardon forgives blame that still stands.
items.example: New forensic evidence exonerated the two men after eleven years.

items.question: Employees may raise a formal ________ if they believe the policy has been applied unfairly.
items.correct: grievance
distractors: petition
appraisal
proposal
items.note: A grievance is a formal complaint within an organisation or against an employer.
items.example: She lodged a grievance about the shift allocation.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Impartial'.
items.correct: Unbiased
distractors: Indifferent
Undecided
Lenient
items.note: Impartial means without favour, not without interest or opinion.
items.example: Every defendant is entitled to an impartial tribunal.

items.question: What is a provision in a contract or statute?
items.correct: A particular clause or condition set out within the text of the document itself
distractors: The overall purpose that the drafters intended the document as a whole to achieve
An amendment added to the document after it has been signed by all of the parties
The introductory section explaining the background against which the document was made
items.note: A provision is one specific clause, not the whole instrument or its purpose.
items.example: The confidentiality provision survives termination of the agreement.

items.question: What does restitution require?
items.correct: Giving back what was wrongfully taken, or paying the owner its equivalent value
distractors: Paying an additional sum designed to punish the wrongdoer for particularly bad conduct
Publishing a formal apology in a national newspaper at the wrongdoer's own expense
Serving a period of unpaid work in the community instead of a custodial sentence
items.note: Restitution restores a gain to its owner; punitive damages punish instead.
items.example: The court ordered restitution of the misappropriated funds.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Compelling' when describing evidence.
items.correct: Weak
distractors: Circumstantial
Disputed
Preliminary
items.note: Compelling evidence forces a conclusion; weak evidence fails to.
items.example: The prosecution presented compelling evidence of the transfers.

items.question: Due to the early detection of the disease, the patient's long-term ________ is excellent.
items.correct: prognosis
distractors: diagnosis
prescription
referral
items.note: A prognosis predicts the likely course; a diagnosis names the condition.
items.example: The prognosis after early surgery is generally very good.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for the medical term 'Benign'.
items.correct: Malignant
distractors: Severe
Contagious
Chronic
items.note: Benign growths do not invade or spread; malignant ones do.
items.example: The biopsy confirmed that the lump was benign.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Chronic'.
items.correct: Acute
distractors: Mild
Curable
Infectious
items.note: Chronic means long-lasting; acute means sudden and short.
items.example: She has been treated for chronic back pain for years.

items.question: What does 'acute' describe in a clinical context?
items.correct: A condition that begins suddenly and lasts only a short time before it resolves
distractors: A condition that develops slowly and persists over a long period of a patient's life
A condition that produces unusually severe pain regardless of how long it has lasted
A condition that appears in several members of the same family across generations
items.note: Acute refers to speed of onset, not to severity.
items.example: He was admitted with acute appendicitis.

items.question: What does 'malignant' indicate about a tumour?
items.correct: That it can invade the surrounding tissue and spread to distant parts of the body
distractors: That it has grown large enough to press painfully against the surrounding organs
That it has returned in the same location after having been surgically removed once
That it produces hormones which disturb the normal chemical balance of the body
items.note: Malignancy is defined by invasion and spread, not by size or pain.
items.example: The cells were found to be malignant on histology.

items.question: What is a contraindication?
items.correct: A reason, based on the patient's condition, why a treatment should not be given
distractors: An unwanted effect that a drug may produce alongside its intended therapeutic action
A sign observed by a clinician that confirms the presence of a suspected disease process
An instruction describing the amount of a drug a patient should take and how often
items.note: A contraindication forbids a treatment; a side effect merely accompanies it.
items.example: Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for this drug.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Prophylaxis'.
items.correct: Prevention
distractors: Treatment
Diagnosis
Recovery
items.note: Prophylaxis acts before disease occurs.
items.example: Antibiotic prophylaxis is standard before this operation.

items.question: What does remission mean?
items.correct: A period during which the signs and symptoms of a disease are reduced or entirely absent
distractors: The complete and permanent elimination of a disease from the body with no possibility of return
The point at which a patient stops responding to the treatment they have been receiving
The stage at which a disease first becomes detectable through routine screening tests
items.note: Remission is not the same as cure; the disease may return.
items.example: She has been in remission for three years.

items.question: Treatment was complicated by significant ________, particularly her diabetes and hypertension.
items.correct: comorbidity
distractors: frailty
anxiety
malnutrition
items.note: Comorbidity means additional diseases present alongside the main one.
items.example: Comorbidity strongly influences surgical risk.

items.question: What does the efficacy of a drug refer to?
items.correct: How reliably it produces the intended result under the controlled conditions of a trial
distractors: How safely it can be taken by patients over a prolonged period without causing harm
How quickly it is absorbed into the bloodstream after being swallowed by the patient
How affordable it is for health systems to supply to large numbers of patients
items.note: Efficacy is measured in trials; effectiveness is measured in real practice.
items.example: The vaccine demonstrated high efficacy in phase three trials.

items.question: What does palliative care aim to do?
items.correct: To relieve symptoms and distress rather than to remove the cause of the illness
distractors: Remove the underlying cause of the illness through surgery or targeted medication
Prevent the illness from developing in patients who are known to be at high risk
Restore the patient to the level of physical function they had before the illness
items.note: Palliative treatment targets comfort, not cure.
items.example: He was referred to the palliative care team.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Lesion'.
items.correct: Damage
distractors: Infection
Inflammation
Symptom
items.note: A lesion is any area of damaged or abnormal tissue.
items.example: The scan revealed a small lesion on the liver.

items.question: What is an incision?
items.correct: A cut made deliberately into the body by a surgeon during a planned operation
distractors: An accidental tear in the skin caused by contact with a sharp or jagged object
A small hole made in order to withdraw a sample of fluid for laboratory analysis
A stitched join used to hold the edges of a surgical wound together while it heals
items.note: An incision is intentional and surgical.
items.example: The surgeon closed the incision with dissolvable sutures.

items.question: Which option best describes a non-invasive procedure?
items.correct: A procedure that does not enter the body or break the skin at any point
distractors: A procedure that enters the body only through a very small cut or puncture in the skin
A procedure carried out without giving the patient any form of general anaesthetic
A procedure that is completed within a single day and needs no overnight hospital stay
items.note: Invasive procedures enter the body; non-invasive ones do not.
items.example: An ultrasound is a non-invasive alternative to biopsy.

items.question: What does 'sterile' mean in a clinical setting?
items.correct: Entirely free from all living micro-organisms, including bacteria and their spores
distractors: Cleaned thoroughly with soap and warm water before being used on a patient
Sealed inside packaging so that it cannot be handled by unauthorised personnel
Made from materials that will not cause an allergic reaction in most patients
items.note: Sterile means no microbes at all, which is stronger than clean.
items.example: Instruments must be sterile before entering the operating field.

items.question: After six months of improvement the patient suffered a ________ and was readmitted.
items.correct: relapse
distractors: remission
recovery
referral
items.note: A relapse is the return of a disease after apparent recovery.
items.example: Stopping the medication early often triggers a relapse.

items.question: What is the purpose of screening?
items.correct: To detect disease at an early stage in people who have not yet developed symptoms
distractors: To confirm a suspected diagnosis in a patient who has already reported clear symptoms
To monitor how well a patient is responding to a course of treatment already started
To decide which of several available treatments is most suitable for an individual
items.note: Screening targets symptom-free populations.
items.example: National screening has reduced deaths from cervical cancer.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Dosage'.
items.correct: Amount
distractors: Strength
Prescription
Route
items.note: Dosage is how much medicine is taken; a dose is a single measured amount.
items.example: The dosage was halved because of her kidney function.

items.question: What does immunity mean in medicine?
items.correct: The ability of the body to resist a particular infection after exposure or vaccination
distractors: The absence of any noticeable symptoms during the early stages of an infectious illness
The speed at which the body clears a drug from the bloodstream after it is taken
The tendency of certain bacteria to survive treatment with commonly used antibiotics
items.note: Immunity is resistance in the host; resistance in the microbe is a different idea.
items.example: Vaccination confers immunity without causing the disease.

items.question: What is inflammation?
items.correct: The body's protective response to injury, causing redness, heat, pain and swelling
distractors: An invasion of body tissue by bacteria, viruses or other harmful micro-organisms
The gradual replacement of healthy tissue by fibrous scar tissue after an injury
An abnormal accumulation of fluid in the spaces between cells in the tissues
items.note: Inflammation is a response; infection is a cause it may respond to.
items.example: Steroids were prescribed to reduce the inflammation.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Lethargy'.
items.correct: Tiredness
distractors: Weakness
Dizziness
Confusion
items.note: Lethargy is abnormal drowsiness and lack of energy.
items.example: Persistent lethargy may indicate an underactive thyroid.

items.question: What is nausea?
items.correct: The unpleasant feeling that one is about to bring up the stomach contents
distractors: The forceful expulsion of the contents of the stomach through the mouth
A spinning sensation experienced when standing up quickly from a seated position
A burning discomfort felt behind the breastbone after eating a large meal
items.note: Nausea is the sensation; vomiting is the act.
items.example: Nausea is a common side effect of chemotherapy.

items.question: What does 'terminal' mean when applied to an illness?
items.correct: Expected to end in death because the disease can no longer be cured by treatment
distractors: Severe enough to require continuous monitoring in an intensive care environment
Affecting the final stages of one particular organ while others remain healthy
Diagnosed at such a late stage that treatment has only just begun to be given
items.note: Terminal describes the expected outcome, not the level of care.
items.example: He was given a diagnosis of terminal illness in March.

items.question: Which option best contrasts with a 'symptom'?
items.correct: Sign
distractors: Complaint
Fatigue
Nausea
items.note: Symptoms are reported by patients; signs are observed by clinicians.
items.example: Fever is a sign, whereas fatigue is a symptom.

items.question: The blood results finally confirmed a ________ of iron-deficiency anaemia.
items.correct: diagnosis
distractors: prognosis
prescription
referral
items.note: A diagnosis identifies the condition; a prognosis forecasts its course.
items.example: An early diagnosis greatly improves survival.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Suture'.
items.correct: Stitch
distractors: Clip
Bandage
Dressing
items.note: A suture is the stitch used to close a wound.
items.example: The sutures will be removed after ten days.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Sedentary'.
items.correct: Active
distractors: Restless
Alert
Anxious
items.note: Sedentary means involving much sitting and little physical activity.
items.example: A sedentary lifestyle raises cardiovascular risk.

items.question: What does anaesthesia produce?
items.correct: A controlled and reversible loss of sensation or of consciousness during surgery
distractors: A reduction in anxiety before an operation without affecting awareness or sensation
A temporary paralysis of the muscles used in breathing during a surgical procedure
A state of deep natural sleep from which the patient can easily be woken by speech
items.note: Anaesthesia removes sensation; sedation only calms the patient.
items.example: The repair was performed under local anaesthesia.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Adverse' in 'adverse reaction'.
items.correct: Harmful
distractors: Unexpected
Delayed
Rare
items.note: Adverse means harmful or unfavourable, whether expected or not.
items.example: Any adverse reaction must be reported to the regulator.

items.question: What does 'hereditary' mean?
items.correct: Transmitted from parents to their children through the genes carried in their cells
distractors: Occurring more frequently among people who live together in the same household
Developing gradually as a result of long-term exposure to an environmental factor
Present at the moment of birth but not caused by any inherited genetic material
items.note: Hereditary means genetically inherited; congenital only means present at birth.
items.example: The condition is hereditary and affects several relatives.

items.question: What does the term 'tensile' refer to in materials science?
items.correct: Relating to the stretching forces that pull a material apart or draw it out lengthwise
distractors: The maximum amount of compressive weight a material can handle before fracturing entirely
The measure of a fluid's resistance to gradual deformation under an applied shearing force
A material's capacity to absorb energy and deform plastically before experiencing structural failure
items.note: Tensile forces pull apart; compressive forces push together.
items.example: Steel cable has extremely high tensile strength.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Feasible' in the context of project planning.
items.correct: Possible
distractors: Desirable
Profitable
Ambitious
items.note: Feasible means practically achievable, not merely desirable.
items.example: A tunnel is technically feasible but prohibitively expensive.

items.question: What does 'tolerance' mean in manufacturing?
items.correct: The amount of variation from the stated dimension that a finished part may have
distractors: The maximum load a finished component can carry before it begins to deform permanently
The degree to which a material resists wear when two surfaces rub against each other
The length of time a part is expected to remain in service before it must be replaced
items.note: Tolerance is allowed error, expressed as a range around a nominal dimension.
items.example: The shaft must be machined to a tolerance of 0.02 mm.

items.question: What is material fatigue?
items.correct: Progressive weakening caused by many repeated cycles of loading and unloading
distractors: A sudden fracture that occurs when a single load exceeds the strength of the material
The gradual loss of material from a surface caused by chemical reaction with the air
A permanent change in shape that remains after a heavy load has been removed
items.note: Fatigue comes from repetition, not from one overload.
items.example: The wing spar failed through metal fatigue after 40,000 cycles.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Calibrate'.
items.correct: Adjust
distractors: Measure
Install
Replace
items.note: To calibrate is to check an instrument against a known standard and adjust it if it reads wrongly.
items.example: The sensors are calibrated every six months.

items.question: What is corrosion?
items.correct: The gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its surroundings
distractors: The wearing away of a surface caused by friction with another moving solid object
The cracking of a material caused by rapid changes between hot and cold conditions
The build-up of mineral deposits inside a pipe that gradually restricts the flow
items.note: Corrosion is chemical; erosion and abrasion are mechanical.
items.example: Galvanising protects the frame against corrosion.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Ductile'.
items.correct: Brittle
distractors: Rigid
Dense
Porous
items.note: Ductile materials stretch before breaking; brittle ones snap.
items.example: Copper is ductile enough to be drawn into fine wire.

items.question: What does redundancy mean in system design?
items.correct: Extra components deliberately included so that the failure of any one is survivable
distractors: Removing parts that are unnecessary in order to reduce the total weight of the system
Designing a system so that every component can be replaced quickly during maintenance
Running a system below its rated capacity so that it lasts longer before wearing out
items.note: Redundancy adds spares deliberately; it is not waste.
items.example: The aircraft has triple redundancy in its hydraulic systems.

items.question: The supplier delivered valves that did not meet the agreed technical ________.
items.correct: specification
distractors: schedule
budget
terminology
items.note: A specification states required properties and performance in detail.
items.example: Every weld must conform to the specification.

items.question: What is torque?
items.correct: A turning or twisting force that tends to make an object rotate about an axis
distractors: The rate at which a machine converts stored energy into useful mechanical work
The straight-line force applied to an object in the direction in which it is moving
The resistance an object offers to any change in its current state of motion
items.note: Torque turns; force pushes; power is work per unit time.
items.example: Tighten the bolts to a torque of 90 newton-metres.

items.question: What does viscosity measure?
items.correct: The resistance a fluid offers to flow, or how thickly and slowly it moves
distractors: The mass contained within each unit of volume of a particular liquid or gas
The temperature at which a liquid begins to change into vapour at normal pressure
The pressure exerted by a liquid on the walls of the container that holds it
items.note: High viscosity means thick and slow-flowing.
items.example: Cold weather raises the viscosity of the lubricant.

items.question: What is the yield point of a material?
items.correct: The level of stress at which it stops behaving elastically and deforms permanently
distractors: The stress at which the material separates into two pieces and can no longer carry load
The proportion of applied energy the material gives back once the load has been removed
The temperature at which the material softens sufficiently to be shaped by forging
items.note: Yield marks the end of elastic behaviour, not the moment of fracture.
items.example: The beam was loaded to just below its yield point.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Prototype'.
items.correct: Model
distractors: Blueprint
Replica
Standard
items.note: A prototype is a first working version built for testing.
items.example: The prototype failed its first vibration test.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Robust' when describing a design.
items.correct: Sturdy
distractors: Rigid
Portable
Elegant
items.note: Robust means able to withstand difficult conditions without failing.
items.example: The housing is robust enough for offshore use.

items.question: What does throughput measure?
items.correct: The quantity of material, product or data that a system actually handles in a given period
distractors: The delay between a request being made and the first part of the response arriving
The largest quantity a system could theoretically handle under perfect operating conditions
The proportion of processed items that meet the required quality standard on inspection
items.note: Throughput is actual rate; capacity is theoretical maximum; latency is delay.
items.example: Automating the sorting stage doubled throughput.

items.question: What is an alloy?
items.correct: A metal made by combining two or more chemical elements, one of them a metal
distractors: A thin protective layer applied to the outside of a metal component to prevent rust
A metal that has been heated and cooled slowly in order to make it easier to work
A naturally occurring rock from which a useful metal can be extracted commercially
items.note: An alloy is a mixture, not a coating or an ore.
items.example: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

items.question: What does deflection describe?
items.correct: The distance a beam or other member bends away from its original position under load
distractors: The total weight that a structural member is designed to carry throughout its service life
The angle at which two structural members meet at a connection within a steel frame
The permanent distortion that remains in a member after the applied load is removed
items.note: Deflection is displacement under load and is usually recoverable.
items.example: Deflection at mid-span must not exceed span over 360.

items.question: What does 'brittle' mean?
items.correct: Liable to snap or crack suddenly under load, with little or no bending beforehand
distractors: Easily bent into a new shape without any risk of the material cracking or breaking
Gradually weakened by long exposure to moisture and to changes in air temperature
Soft enough to be marked or scratched by contact with a harder material surface
items.note: Brittle materials fail with little or no plastic deformation.
items.example: Cast iron is strong in compression but brittle.

items.question: What is the purpose of insulation?
items.correct: To slow or block the transfer of heat, sound or electricity across a boundary
distractors: To increase the speed at which heat moves away from a component that is running hot
To prevent moisture from reaching a surface that would otherwise begin to corrode
To absorb the energy of an impact so that the structure behind it is not damaged
items.note: Insulation blocks transfer; a conductor promotes it.
items.example: Poor insulation accounts for most of the heat loss.

items.question: A system with very low latency is best described as ________.
items.correct: Responsive
distractors: Scalable
Reliable
Affordable
items.note: Latency is delay; low latency means a fast response, not high volume.
items.example: Remote surgery demands latency below fifty milliseconds.

items.question: What does a modular design mean?
items.correct: Built from separate standardised units that can be combined or exchanged freely
distractors: Produced in very large quantities so that the cost of each unit falls considerably
Made entirely from a single piece of material with no joints or fastenings at all
Designed so that the appearance can be customised to suit individual customers
items.note: Modularity is about interchangeable units, not mass production.
items.example: The modular racks can be reconfigured in an afternoon.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Optimise'.
items.correct: Improve
distractors: Simplify
Automate
Postpone
items.note: To optimise is to make as effective as possible within constraints.
items.example: The route was optimised to cut fuel consumption.

items.question: What is the payload of a vehicle?
items.correct: The weight of the useful cargo or equipment that a vehicle is designed to carry
distractors: The total weight of the vehicle including its own structure, fuel and everything on board
The maximum weight the vehicle is legally permitted to place on any single axle
The weight of fuel required for the vehicle to complete its longest planned journey
items.note: Payload excludes the vehicle's own mass.
items.example: The drone has a payload of just two kilograms.

items.question: Which term is most often contrasted with 'precision' in measurement?
items.correct: Accuracy
distractors: Resolution
Sensitivity
Stability
items.note: Precision is repeatability; accuracy is closeness to the true value.
items.example: The gauge is precise but consistently reads two microns high.

items.question: What does it mean to retrofit a building or machine?
items.correct: To install new components or systems in a building or machine already in service
distractors: To restore something to the exact condition it was in when it was originally built
To dismantle something completely so that its materials can be recovered and reused
To replace an ageing installation entirely with a newly manufactured equivalent
items.note: Retrofitting upgrades existing assets rather than restoring or replacing them.
items.example: The plant was retrofitted with heat-recovery units.

items.question: What is a shear force?
items.correct: A force that makes adjacent layers of a material slide past one another sideways
distractors: A force that squeezes a material and reduces its overall length along one axis
A force that pulls a material apart and increases its length along a single axis
A force that causes a member to twist about its own longitudinal centre line
items.note: Shear acts sideways across a section, unlike tension or compression.
items.example: The bolts failed in shear rather than in tension.

items.question: What is stress in a loaded component?
items.correct: The internal force within a loaded part, measured over each unit of cross-section
distractors: The change in length of the component divided by its original unloaded length
The total external load applied to the component measured in newtons or kilograms
The energy stored inside the component while it is being held in a deformed state
items.note: Stress is force per area; strain is the resulting relative deformation.
items.example: Stress concentrates sharply at the corner of the opening.

items.question: What does 'sustainable' mean in engineering practice?
items.correct: Able to continue over the long term without exhausting resources or harming the future
distractors: Built from materials that have already been recovered from other products or structures
Designed to remain in service for considerably longer than comparable existing designs
Produced at a cost low enough for developing economies to adopt the technology widely
items.note: Sustainability concerns long-term resource and environmental viability.
items.example: Sustainable design considers the whole life cycle of a product.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Thermal'.
items.correct: Heat-related
distractors: Fire-related
Light-related
Motion-related
items.note: Thermal simply means relating to heat or temperature.
items.example: Thermal expansion must be allowed for in the joints.

items.question: Excessive ________ from the compressor was loosening the mounting bolts.
items.correct: vibration
distractors: noise
pressure
condensation
items.note: Vibration is rapid back-and-forth motion and a common cause of fatigue failure.
items.example: Rubber mounts damp the vibration from the motor.

items.question: The merger proved highly ________, generating millions in unexpected profit during the first quarter.
items.correct: lucrative
distractors: expensive
disruptive
complicated
items.note: Lucrative means producing a great deal of profit.
items.example: Licensing turned out to be the most lucrative part of the business.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Deficit'.
items.correct: Surplus
distractors: Reserve
Discount
Turnover
items.note: A deficit is a shortfall; a surplus is an excess.
items.example: The department ended the year with a small deficit.

items.question: What does liquidity measure?
items.correct: How quickly and easily a business can turn the assets it holds into available cash
distractors: The total value of everything a company owns once its debts have been fully subtracted
The proportion of a company's funding that comes from borrowing rather than from owners
The speed at which a company collects payment from customers after issuing an invoice
items.note: Liquidity is about convertibility to cash, not overall wealth.
items.example: The firm is profitable but has a serious liquidity problem.

items.question: What does financial leverage refer to?
items.correct: The use of borrowed money to increase the potential returns on an investment
distractors: The bargaining advantage one party holds in a negotiation over the terms of a contract
The proportion of profits that a company chooses to distribute to its shareholders
The extent to which a company depends on a single customer for most of its income
items.note: In finance, leverage means debt used to amplify returns and risk.
items.example: High leverage left the group exposed when rates rose.

items.question: What are overheads?
items.correct: The continuing costs of running a business that no one product or job accounts for
distractors: The cost of the raw materials and labour used directly in making each individual unit
One-off payments made to acquire buildings, vehicles or equipment for long-term use
Amounts set aside each year to cover debts that customers are unlikely to ever pay
items.note: Overheads are indirect costs such as rent, insurance and administration.
items.example: Moving online cut our overheads by a third.

items.question: Who is a stakeholder?
items.correct: Any person or group affected by, or with an interest in, what an organisation does
distractors: A person who has purchased shares and therefore owns part of the company concerned
A member of the senior management team responsible for setting the company's strategy
An outside consultant hired to give independent advice on a particular business problem
items.note: Every shareholder is a stakeholder, but stakeholders include staff, customers and communities.
items.example: The plan was circulated to all stakeholders for comment.

items.question: What does turnover normally mean in British business English?
items.correct: The total value of sales a business makes in a period, before costs are deducted
distractors: The amount of money remaining once all of the company's costs have been deducted
The total value of goods held in the warehouse and available for immediate delivery
The proportion of a market that one particular company has managed to capture
items.note: Turnover is revenue before costs; profit is what remains after them.
items.example: Annual turnover passed 200 million baht for the first time.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Diversify'.
items.correct: Broaden
distractors: Restructure
Merge
Automate
items.note: To diversify is to widen the range of products, markets or investments.
items.example: The group diversified into logistics after the downturn.

items.question: What does procurement involve?
items.correct: The sourcing, negotiating and buying of the goods and services an organisation needs
distractors: Storing and organising inventory so that items can be located quickly when required
Delivering finished products from the warehouse to customers within an agreed period
Deciding the price at which the organisation will sell its products to the public
items.note: Procurement covers sourcing, negotiating and buying.
items.example: Public procurement rules require open tendering.

items.question: Rising freight costs squeezed the company's profit ________ to under four per cent.
items.correct: margin
distractors: forecast
target
allocation
items.note: Margin is profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
items.example: Supermarkets operate on very thin margins.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Incentive'.
items.correct: Motivation
distractors: Requirement
Restriction
Explanation
items.note: An incentive encourages a particular behaviour, often financially.
items.example: Bonuses were introduced as an incentive to hit targets.

items.question: What is a merger?
items.correct: Two separate companies joining their operations together to form one single business
distractors: One company buying enough shares in another to take control of it against its wishes
An agreement between two companies to work together on one project without combining
The division of a large company into several smaller independently managed businesses
items.note: A merger joins equals; an acquisition means one company absorbs another.
items.example: The merger created the region's largest logistics operator.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Liability' in accounting.
items.correct: Asset
distractors: Expense
Revenue
Reserve
items.note: Liabilities are what a business owes; assets are what it owns.
items.example: Pension obligations are the group's largest liability.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Forecast'.
items.correct: Prediction
distractors: Target
Record
Summary
items.note: A forecast projects what is likely; a target states what is intended.
items.example: The sales forecast was revised downwards in June.

items.question: What is a benchmark?
items.correct: An agreed reference point against which performance can be measured and compared
distractors: An ambitious goal that an organisation sets itself for the coming financial period
A detailed review of a competitor's products carried out by the marketing department
The minimum acceptable level of quality below which a product cannot be sold
items.note: A benchmark is a reference point for comparison, not a goal.
items.example: We benchmark our delivery times against the industry leader.

items.question: What does staff attrition refer to?
items.correct: The gradual shrinking of a workforce as staff leave voluntarily and are not replaced
distractors: The formal dismissal of employees whose performance has fallen below the required level
The reduction of a workforce through planned redundancies announced by management
The transfer of employees between departments in response to changing business needs
items.note: Attrition is natural wastage, distinct from redundancy or dismissal.
items.example: Headcount was reduced through attrition rather than layoffs.

items.question: What does it mean to outsource a function?
items.correct: To pay an outside company to carry out work previously done by your own staff
distractors: To move a department to a country where wages and operating costs are much lower
To automate a routine process so that far fewer employees are needed to complete it
To share responsibility for a task between two departments within the same company
items.note: Outsourcing is about who does the work, not where it is done.
items.example: Payroll has been outsourced to a specialist provider.

items.question: What does equity mean in company finance?
items.correct: The owners' residual interest in a business once all its liabilities are subtracted
distractors: The total amount of money that the company has borrowed from banks and bondholders
The cash the company holds in its accounts and can spend immediately if it needs to
The value of the buildings, machinery and vehicles that the company currently owns
items.note: Equity is owners' residual claim: assets minus liabilities.
items.example: The founders retained sixty per cent of the equity.

items.question: What is depreciation in a company's accounts?
items.correct: The practice of spreading the cost of an asset across the years of its useful life
distractors: A fall in the value of a currency compared with the currencies of other countries
A reduction in the selling price of goods that have been in stock for a long time
The loss of value a product suffers as soon as a newer version is released
items.note: In accounting, depreciation allocates cost across periods.
items.example: After depreciation the fleet is worth half what we paid.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Viable' when describing a business.
items.correct: Workable
distractors: Profitable
Innovative
Established
items.note: Viable means capable of surviving and working in practice.
items.example: The branch is no longer commercially viable.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Consolidate'.
items.correct: Combine
distractors: Reorganise
Divide
Postpone
items.note: To consolidate is to bring separate things together into one stronger whole.
items.example: The three regional offices were consolidated into one.

items.question: What is a quota?
items.correct: A fixed limit or share of something allocated to a particular person or group
distractors: A financial reward paid to staff who exceed the results expected of them in a period
An estimate of how much a team is likely to sell during the coming three months
A written agreement guaranteeing a supplier a certain volume of orders each year
items.note: A quota fixes an amount, whether a maximum permitted or a minimum required.
items.example: Each sales rep must meet a monthly quota.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Remuneration'.
items.correct: Payment
distractors: Reimbursement
Recognition
Promotion
items.note: Remuneration is the formal word for total pay, including benefits.
items.example: The remuneration committee reviews executive pay annually.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Solvent' in a financial sense.
items.correct: Bankrupt
distractors: Illiquid
Indebted
Unprofitable
items.note: Solvent means able to pay debts as they fall due; the direct opposite is insolvent, and bankruptcy is the legal outcome of insolvency.
items.example: The rescue package kept the airline solvent.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Streamline'.
items.correct: Simplify
distractors: Accelerate
Expand
Outsource
items.note: To streamline is to make a process more efficient by removing steps.
items.example: We streamlined approvals from six stages to two.

items.question: What is a subsidiary?
items.correct: A company whose management is controlled by another, larger company that owns it
distractors: A separate business set up jointly by two companies that each own half of the shares
A local office of a company that has no legal identity of its own in that country
An independent supplier that sells almost all of its output to one large customer
items.note: A subsidiary is a separate company under the control of a parent.
items.example: The Thai subsidiary files its own accounts.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Volatile' when describing a market.
items.correct: Stable
distractors: Sluggish
Regulated
Crowded
items.note: Volatile means changing rapidly and unpredictably in either direction.
items.example: Commodity prices remain extremely volatile.

items.question: What is a dividend?
items.correct: A share of a company's profits paid out to the people who own its shares
distractors: The increase in the market price of a share since the day it was originally bought
The interest a company pays to the banks and bondholders who have lent it money
The fee charged by a broker for arranging the purchase or the sale of shares
items.note: Dividends come from profit; capital gain comes from a rising share price.
items.example: The board suspended the dividend to preserve cash.

items.question: What does a franchise arrangement involve?
items.correct: Paying for the right to trade under an established brand and its business system
distractors: Buying a controlling interest in an existing business together with all of its premises
Agreeing to sell another company's products alongside your own in your existing shops
Licensing a patented technology so that it can be used in your own manufacturing
items.note: A franchisee buys the right to run a business under someone else's brand and rules.
items.example: She owns three franchises of a coffee chain.

items.question: The tenant fell three months into ________ and received a formal demand.
items.correct: arrears
distractors: default
dispute
negotiation
items.note: Arrears are overdue payments; the fixed phrase is to fall into arrears.
items.example: Rent arrears rose sharply during the recession.

items.question: What does syntax describe?
items.correct: The rules governing the ways in which words may be combined to form grammatical sentences
distractors: The system of rules that determines the meanings carried by individual words and phrases
The set of speech sounds that a particular language uses to distinguish one word from another
The conventions governing how a language is written down, including spelling and punctuation
items.note: Syntax is sentence structure; semantics is meaning.
items.example: Thai and English differ sharply in their syntax.

items.question: What is a cognate?
items.correct: A word that shares a common historical origin with a related word in another language
distractors: A word borrowed directly from another language and used without any change in spelling
A word that looks similar in two languages but carries a completely different meaning
A word invented recently to describe a technology that did not previously exist
items.note: Cognates share ancestry; false friends only look alike.
items.example: English 'father' and German 'Vater' are cognates.

items.question: What does fluency refer to in language assessment?
items.correct: The ability to speak or write smoothly, at a natural pace and without undue hesitation
distractors: The ability to use a wide range of vocabulary precisely and appropriately in context
The ability to produce grammatically correct sentences without making any errors at all
The ability to pronounce every sound in the language exactly as a native speaker would
items.note: Fluency is about flow and pace, not accuracy or range.
items.example: Her fluency improved far faster than her accuracy.

items.question: What is an idiom?
items.correct: A fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot be worked out from its separate words
distractors: A short saying that offers a piece of traditional wisdom or practical everyday advice
A fixed pair of words that native speakers habitually use together in that exact order
A word or phrase used only by a particular profession and rarely understood outside it
items.note: Idioms are non-literal; collocations are simply habitual pairings.
items.example: 'Bite the bullet' is an idiom, not a literal instruction.

items.question: What is a morpheme?
items.correct: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning of its own and cannot be split further
distractors: The smallest unit of sound capable of distinguishing one word in a language from another
A group of words that functions as a single unit within the structure of a larger sentence
The basic form of a word as it appears when it is listed in a standard printed dictionary
items.note: Morphemes carry meaning; phonemes distinguish sound.
items.example: 'Unhappiness' contains three morphemes.

items.question: What is a phoneme?
items.correct: A unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another within a particular language
distractors: The smallest part of a word that carries meaning of its own, such as a prefix or ending
A single letter of the alphabet as it is written down in the standard spelling system
The pattern of rising and falling pitch used across a whole spoken phrase or sentence
items.note: Swapping a phoneme changes the word: pat becomes bat.
items.example: English has around forty-four phonemes.

items.question: What does register mean in linguistics?
items.correct: The level of formality and the style that suit a particular situation or audience
distractors: The regional variety of a language spoken by people living in one particular area
The written record kept of all the words that a learner has met and needs to know
The degree of grammatical complexity found in a piece of written or spoken language
items.note: Register is formality and appropriacy; dialect is regional variety.
items.example: Contractions are wrong for the register of an academic essay.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 meaning of 'Bilingual'.
items.correct: Speaking two languages
distractors: Studying languages
Interpreting conversations
Travelling widely
items.note: Bilingual describes the speaker, not the activity of translating.
items.example: The school offers a bilingual programme in Thai and English.

items.question: Identify the best term contrasted with 'Connotation'.
items.correct: Denotation
distractors: Derivation
Pronunciation
Abbreviation
items.note: Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the feeling attached.
items.example: 'Thrifty' and 'stingy' share a denotation but not a connotation.

items.question: What is a dialect?
items.correct: A variety of a language particular to one region or to one social group of speakers
distractors: A way of pronouncing a language that shows where the speaker originally comes from
A completely separate language that happens to share some vocabulary with a neighbour
A simplified form of a language used between speakers who share no common tongue
items.note: A dialect includes grammar and vocabulary; an accent is pronunciation only.
items.example: The northern dialect uses several distinct verb forms.

items.question: What does etymology study?
items.correct: The study of where words came from and of how their forms and meanings have changed
distractors: The way in which the meanings of words relate to one another within a single language
The rules that determine which sounds may follow one another inside a spoken word
The differences between the vocabulary used by younger and older groups of speakers
items.note: Etymology traces word history.
items.example: The etymology of 'salary' goes back to Roman payments in salt.

items.question: What is inflection in grammar?
items.correct: A change in the form of a word that marks grammatical tense, number, person or case
distractors: The addition of a prefix to a word in order to create a new word with a different meaning
The rise and fall of the voice used to signal a question rather than a plain statement
The combining of two separate words to form a single compound with a new meaning
items.note: Inflection changes grammatical form, not the core meaning.
items.example: 'Walked' shows past-tense inflection.

items.question: What is intonation?
items.correct: The way in which the pitch of the voice rises and falls across a phrase or sentence
distractors: The relative loudness given to one syllable compared with the others in the same word
The speed at which a speaker produces words during a stretch of continuous speech
The clarity with which individual consonant sounds are produced at the end of words
items.note: Intonation is pitch movement across a phrase; stress is syllable prominence.
items.example: Rising intonation can turn a statement into a question.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Lexicon'.
items.correct: Vocabulary
distractors: Grammar
Alphabet
Pronunciation
items.note: A lexicon is the whole word stock of a language or a person.
items.example: Technical terms have entered the everyday lexicon.

items.question: What does literacy mean?
items.correct: The ability to read and to write with reasonable competence in a given language
distractors: The ability to speak a language confidently in a range of everyday social situations
The level of formal education a person has completed in schools or in universities
Familiarity with the great novels and poems written in a particular language
items.note: Literacy is the reading and writing skill itself.
items.example: Adult literacy rates have risen steadily since 1990.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Nuance'.
items.correct: Subtlety
distractors: Ambiguity
Emphasis
Exaggeration
items.note: A nuance is a fine shade of difference in meaning or feeling.
items.example: Machine translation still misses nuance.

items.question: What does orthography cover?
items.correct: The conventional system used for writing down and spelling a particular language
distractors: The set of sounds used by a language and the way they are produced by the speaker
The rules that govern the order in which words may be arranged inside a sentence
The way a language marks differences of politeness between speakers of different rank
items.note: Orthography concerns writing and spelling conventions.
items.example: Thai orthography does not mark spaces between words.

items.question: What does it mean to paraphrase a text?
items.correct: To express the same meaning again using wording quite different from the original
distractors: To reduce it to a much shorter version that keeps only the most important points
To copy the original wording exactly while acknowledging clearly where it came from
To translate it accurately from one language into another without changing meaning
items.note: Paraphrasing restates the same meaning in new wording; summarising also cuts the content down.
items.example: Candidates must paraphrase the prompt in the introduction.

items.question: What does pragmatics study?
items.correct: The study of how the situation and context shape the meaning of what a speaker says
distractors: How the meanings of words and sentences are built up from their individual parts
How the sound system of a language organises consonants, vowels and syllable patterns
How languages change over long periods of time as they are passed between generations
items.note: Pragmatics is meaning in use: implication, politeness, intent.
items.example: 'Can you open the window?' is a request, as pragmatics explains.

items.question: Identify the best antonym for 'Prescriptive' in grammar.
items.correct: Descriptive
distractors: Historical
Comparative
Practical
items.note: Prescriptive rules state how people should speak; descriptive ones record how they do.
items.example: 'Never split an infinitive' is a prescriptive rule.

items.question: Semantics is the study of ________.
items.correct: meaning
distractors: structure
pronunciation
sound
items.note: Semantics deals with meaning in words and sentences.
items.example: The dispute is one of semantics rather than of fact.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Colloquial'.
items.correct: Formal
distractors: Written
Regional
Poetic
items.note: Colloquial language is informal and conversational.
items.example: Avoid colloquial expressions in Task 2 writing.

items.question: What does language acquisition refer to?
items.correct: The process, largely unconscious, by which a person comes to know and use a language
distractors: The deliberate study of grammar rules and vocabulary lists inside a formal classroom
The gradual loss of a first language after long residence in a foreign speaking country
The testing of a learner's ability in order to place them at the correct level of a course
items.note: Acquisition is often contrasted with conscious learning.
items.example: First-language acquisition is largely complete by age five.

items.question: What is ambiguity in a sentence?
items.correct: The possibility that a reader can quite properly understand it in more than one way
distractors: The use of words that are too abstract for the reader to picture anything concrete
The presence of a grammatical error that makes the sentence impossible to understand
The deliberate omission of information that the writer expects the reader to supply
items.note: Ambiguity means two or more readings are genuinely available.
items.example: 'Visiting relatives can be tiring' is structurally ambiguous.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Articulate' describing a speaker.
items.correct: Well-spoken
distractors: Knowledgeable
Confident
Multilingual
items.note: Articulate means expressing ideas clearly and effectively.
items.example: She is an unusually articulate advocate for the policy.

items.question: What does coherence mean in writing?
items.correct: That the ideas of a text are ordered logically so that the argument is easy to follow
distractors: That the sentences are joined by suitable linking words such as however and therefore
That the grammar and spelling throughout the text are accurate and free from errors
That the vocabulary chosen is varied enough to avoid repeating the same words often
items.note: Coherence is logical flow of ideas; cohesion is the surface linking devices.
items.example: The essay has cohesion but lacks overall coherence.

items.question: What is a collocation?
items.correct: A pair of words that habitually occur together and therefore sound natural to speakers
distractors: An expression whose overall meaning is quite different from the meanings of its words
Two words that sound identical to each other but are spelled differently and mean different things
A word that has been borrowed into English from another language relatively recently
items.note: Collocations are natural pairings such as 'heavy rain'.
items.example: 'Make a decision' is a collocation; 'do a decision' is not.

items.question: What does 'discourse' refer to in linguistics?
items.correct: Language examined in stretches longer than a sentence, such as whole conversations
distractors: A formal debate held between two speakers who hold opposing views on a single topic
The vocabulary and grammar particular to one academic subject or professional field
A written record of everything that was said during a conversation or an interview
items.note: Discourse analysis looks at whole texts and conversations.
items.example: Discourse markers help listeners follow the argument.

items.question: What does immersion mean in language teaching?
items.correct: Learning a language by being surrounded by it and using it for other subjects
distractors: Studying a language intensively for several hours each day over a short concentrated period
Learning a language mainly through reading literature written by native authors
Practising a language with a partner who is a native speaker of that language
items.note: Immersion means the language is the medium, not just the subject.
items.example: The immersion programme teaches science entirely in English.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Vernacular'.
items.correct: Everyday language
distractors: Formal standard
Ceremonial language
Archaic speech
items.note: The vernacular is the ordinary language of a place or people.
items.example: The Bible was eventually translated into the vernacular.

items.question: What does sovereignty mean?
items.correct: The supreme legal authority that a state exercises over its own territory and population
distractors: The right of a people sharing a culture to govern themselves as an independent nation
The recognition granted to a new government by the other members of the international community
The power of a national parliament to pass laws without approval from the head of state
items.note: Sovereignty is supreme authority; recognition is other states acknowledging it.
items.example: Membership of the bloc involves pooling some sovereignty.

items.question: What is a referendum?
items.correct: A direct vote in which the electorate is asked to decide a single question of policy
distractors: An election in which citizens choose the representatives who will sit in the legislature
A formal survey of public opinion carried out by an independent polling organisation
A debate held in parliament at the end of which members vote on a proposed law
items.note: A referendum asks the electorate about an issue, not about candidates.
items.example: The constitution was approved by referendum in 2017.

items.question: What is a coalition government?
items.correct: A government formed jointly by two or more parties which share the cabinet posts
distractors: A government that continues in office temporarily until a new one has been formed
A government made up of experts rather than of elected politicians from any party
A government formed by the largest single party acting entirely on its own
items.note: A coalition shares cabinet power between parties.
items.example: The coalition collapsed after the smaller party withdrew.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Autocracy'.
items.correct: Democracy
distractors: Theocracy
Federation
Monarchy
items.note: Autocracy concentrates power in one ruler; democracy disperses it to the people.
items.example: The reforms did little to soften the autocracy.

items.question: What does political legitimacy refer to?
items.correct: The general belief among the governed that a government has the right to exercise power
distractors: The legal authority granted to a government by the written constitution of the country
The practical ability of a government to enforce its decisions throughout its territory
The length of time a government has remained continuously in office without interruption
items.note: Legitimacy is about acceptance; legality and capacity are different things.
items.example: The disputed count undermined the government's legitimacy.

items.question: What is a constituency?
items.correct: A defined electoral district whose voters elect one or more members of parliament
distractors: The total number of citizens who are legally entitled to vote in a national election
The local office from which a member of parliament deals with voters' problems
An organised group that campaigns to influence government policy on a single issue
items.note: A constituency is a defined electoral district.
items.example: She has represented the constituency for twelve years.

items.question: What is a political ideology?
items.correct: A connected set of beliefs and values about how society ought to be organised and run
distractors: A detailed programme of measures a party promises to introduce if it wins the election
The personal opinions of an individual politician on the major questions of the day
A strategy designed to win support from voters who have not yet decided how to vote
items.note: An ideology is a belief system; a manifesto is a policy programme.
items.example: The party has drifted from its founding ideology.

items.question: In political science, what does 'the bureaucracy' of a state refer to?
items.correct: The body of appointed officials who administer the policies and services of a government
distractors: The complicated official procedures that make dealing with government slow and frustrating
The elected ministers who take collective responsibility for the decisions of government
The independent judges who decide whether official decisions comply with the law
items.note: Bureaucracy is the administrative apparatus; 'red tape' is the frustration it causes.
items.example: Reform of the bureaucracy has been promised repeatedly.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Suffrage'.
items.correct: The right to vote
distractors: The right to protest
The duty to serve
The freedom to assemble
items.note: Suffrage is the franchise: entitlement to vote.
items.example: Universal suffrage was not achieved until the last century.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Partisan'.
items.correct: Neutral
distractors: Critical
Apathetic
Loyal
items.note: Partisan means strongly favouring one side.
items.example: The commission was accused of partisan appointments.

items.question: Who is the incumbent?
items.correct: The person who is currently holding the office that is being contested at an election
distractors: The candidate expected by most commentators to win the forthcoming election contest
The person who held the office immediately before the current holder took it over
The official appointed to run the administration temporarily until an election is held
items.note: The incumbent holds the post now, whatever their prospects.
items.example: The incumbent enjoys a significant advantage in name recognition.

items.question: What is an electoral mandate?
items.correct: The authority to govern along particular lines that the voters are held to have granted
distractors: A formal instruction issued by a court requiring a public body to take specific action
A binding agreement between coalition partners setting out the policies they will pursue
The fixed period of time for which a parliament sits before elections must be held again
items.note: A mandate is popular authorisation for a programme.
items.example: The government claims a mandate for constitutional reform.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Ratify'.
items.correct: Approve
distractors: Negotiate
Publish
Draft
items.note: Ratification is the formal domestic approval that makes a treaty binding.
items.example: Parliament has yet to ratify the agreement.

items.question: What are sanctions in international politics?
items.correct: Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a state to force a change in the way it acts
distractors: Formal statements condemning the actions of a state without imposing any real penalty
Financial contributions given to a state in return for agreeing to change its policies
Legal proceedings brought against a state before an international court of justice
items.note: Note the trap: 'sanction' as a verb can also mean to approve.
items.example: Trade sanctions were tightened after the crackdown.

items.question: What does federalism involve?
items.correct: A system in which power is divided constitutionally between national and regional government
distractors: The transfer of certain powers from a central government to regional bodies it created
A union of fully independent states that cooperate without giving up any of their sovereignty
A system in which all authority is concentrated in a single national government
items.note: In federalism regional powers are constitutionally guaranteed, not merely delegated.
items.example: German federalism gives the Länder substantial autonomy.

items.question: What does it mean to lobby a government?
items.correct: To try to influence the decisions it takes on behalf of a particular interest group
distractors: To organise a public demonstration in order to show opposition to a proposed policy
To take legal action challenging the lawfulness of a decision that has been made
To provide financial support to a political party during an election campaign period
items.note: Lobbying is direct persuasion of decision-makers.
items.example: Manufacturers lobbied hard against the new emissions rules.

items.question: What characterises populism?
items.correct: A style of politics that sets ordinary people against an elite portrayed as corrupt
distractors: Adopting whichever policies are shown by opinion polls to be the most popular ones
Governing in the interests of the majority while protecting the rights of minorities
Encouraging citizens to take part directly in making decisions about local services
items.note: Populism frames politics as the pure people against a corrupt elite.
items.example: Economic insecurity fuelled the rise of populism.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Secular'.
items.correct: Religious
distractors: Traditional
Ancient
Monarchical
items.note: Secular means separate from religion, not hostile to it.
items.example: The constitution establishes a secular state.

items.question: What is a veto?
items.correct: The power held by a single participant to block a proposed decision outright, on its own
distractors: The right to demand that a decision be reconsidered by the body that originally made it
The ability to delay a decision until further evidence has been presented for discussion
The requirement that a decision be supported by more than half of those entitled to vote
items.note: A veto blocks outright; a delay only postpones.
items.example: Any permanent member can veto the resolution.

items.question: What does 'bipartisan' describe?
items.correct: Something supported jointly by both of the main opposing groupings in a legislature
distractors: A political system in which only two parties have any realistic chance of taking power
A policy that has been deliberately designed to avoid taking any position on a divisive issue
An agreement reached between the government and organisations outside parliament
items.note: Bipartisan means cross-party support, not a two-party system.
items.example: The bill passed with rare bipartisan support.

items.question: What is censorship?
items.correct: The official suppression of speech, writing or images judged to be politically unacceptable
distractors: The legal requirement that broadcasters give equal coverage to all the main political parties
The practice of editing a text to correct its errors before it is published to the public
The classification of official documents as secret in order to protect national security
items.note: Censorship suppresses expression; classification restricts official information.
items.example: Wartime censorship extended to private letters.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Dissent'.
items.correct: Agreement
distractors: Silence
Loyalty
Obedience
items.note: Dissent is the expression of disagreement with an official view.
items.example: Public dissent was met with arrests.

items.question: Turnout fell sharply, with barely half of the ________ casting a vote.
items.correct: electorate
distractors: membership
legislature
judiciary
items.note: The electorate is everyone entitled to vote.
items.example: The electorate has grown by two million since the last poll.

items.question: What does it mean to impeach an official?
items.correct: To bring a formal charge of serious misconduct against them while they still hold office
distractors: To remove them from office immediately after a vote of no confidence has been passed
To investigate their conduct privately before deciding whether any action should be taken
To bar them from ever standing for public office again following a criminal conviction
items.note: Impeachment is the charge; removal only follows conviction.
items.example: The assembly voted to impeach the governor.

items.question: What is nationalism?
items.correct: Strong identification with one's own country and the active promotion of its interests
distractors: A love of one's own country combined with respect for the traditions of other countries
The belief that all political power should be held by the central government of a state
The policy of keeping a country out of foreign conflicts and alliances altogether
items.note: Nationalism prioritises the nation's interests, often above others'.
items.example: Economic nationalism shaped the trade policy.

items.question: What is an oligarchy?
items.correct: A form of government in which power rests with a small and privileged group of people
distractors: Rule by a single individual who has taken power by force and governs without any limits
Rule by officials selected for their expertise rather than elected by the general public
Rule by the whole body of citizens, who decide public questions by direct vote
items.note: Oligarchy means the few rule, however they qualify.
items.example: Critics say the reforms entrenched an oligarchy.

items.question: What does political polarisation describe?
items.correct: The movement of public opinion away from the centre toward two sharply opposed extremes
distractors: A steady decline in the proportion of citizens who take any interest in political questions
The concentration of political power in the hands of a very small number of institutions
The formation of many small parties none of which can command a working majority
items.note: Polarisation is division into two hostile camps, not fragmentation.
