items.example: Social media is often blamed for rising polarisation.

items.question: What is propaganda?
items.correct: Material circulated deliberately and systematically in order to promote a political cause
distractors: Information that is simply false and has been circulated without any deliberate intention
Advertising paid for by a political party during an officially regulated campaign period
Reporting that shows bias because of the personal views of the journalist who wrote it
items.note: Propaganda is purposeful persuasion, true or false.
items.example: State television broadcast propaganda throughout the conflict.

items.question: What is a quorum?
items.correct: The minimum number of members who must attend for a decision to count as valid
distractors: The proportion of votes a proposal must receive before it can be formally adopted
The maximum number of members permitted to attend a closed session of a committee
The list of members formally entitled to speak during a debate in the chamber
items.note: Quorum concerns attendance; a threshold concerns votes cast.
items.example: The meeting was abandoned for want of a quorum.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Repeal'.
items.correct: Enact
distractors: Amend
Enforce
Interpret
items.note: To repeal is to cancel a law; to enact is to bring one into force.
items.example: Parliament voted to repeal the emergency powers.

items.question: What does composition mean in visual art?
items.correct: The way in which the elements of a picture are arranged and balanced within its frame
distractors: The combination of pigments and binders used to create a particular paint or colour
The overall subject matter that the artist has chosen to represent in the finished work
The sequence of stages an artist follows from initial sketch through to final varnish
items.note: Composition is arrangement and balance within the frame.
items.example: The diagonal composition draws the eye to the figure.

items.question: What is perspective in drawing?
items.correct: A technique for representing three-dimensional depth convincingly on a flat surface
distractors: The use of light and shadow to make objects appear rounded and solid on the page
The careful measurement of a subject's proportions before any drawing is begun
The relative size of the figures compared with the objects surrounding them in a scene
items.note: Perspective creates the illusion of three dimensions.
items.example: Renaissance painters mastered linear perspective.

items.question: In discussing an artist's style, what does their palette refer to?
items.correct: The particular range of colours that an artist habitually chooses to work with
distractors: The particular type of paint an artist prefers, such as oil, acrylic or watercolour
The collection of brushes and tools kept ready in the studio during a working session
The overall degree of brightness and contrast found in a finished painting
items.note: Palette means both the mixing board and, figuratively, the colour range.
items.example: His late palette narrowed to blues and greys.

items.question: What is chiaroscuro?
items.correct: The contrast between areas of light and deep shadow used to model form dramatically
distractors: The technique of blending colours so gradually that no edges between them are visible
The application of thick paint so that the marks of the brush remain clearly visible
The use of a single colour in many different tones throughout an entire composition
items.note: Chiaroscuro is dramatic light-dark modelling, as in Caravaggio.
items.example: The chiaroscuro lends the scene a theatrical intensity.

items.question: Identify the best antonym for 'Figurative' art.
items.correct: Abstract
distractors: Decorative
Modern
Photographic
items.note: Figurative art depicts recognisable things; abstract art does not.
items.example: He returned to figurative painting in the 1970s.

items.question: What does abstract art do?
items.correct: Uses shape, line and colour for their own sake, without depicting any recognisable object
distractors: Simplifies real subjects into basic shapes while keeping them clearly identifiable to viewers
Represents ideas and emotions through symbols that stand for something other than themselves
Depicts imaginary scenes that could never actually occur in the ordinary physical world
items.note: Pure abstraction has no representational subject at all.
items.example: Her abstract canvases explore rhythm and interval.

items.question: What does a curator do?
items.correct: Chooses works, researches them and arranges them in a collection or public exhibition
distractors: Repairs and cleans damaged works so that they can safely be put back on public display
Values works of art for insurance purposes and for sale at auction to private buyers
Writes reviews of exhibitions for newspapers and specialist art magazines and journals
items.note: Curating is selection, interpretation and display.
items.example: The curator hung the early works chronologically.

items.question: The city awarded the sculptor a ________ for a memorial in the central square.
items.correct: commission
distractors: grant
sponsorship
prize
items.note: A commission is a paid order for a specific new work.
items.example: The altarpiece was a private commission.

items.question: What does 'medium' mean in art?
items.correct: The material or the technique that an artist uses to make a particular work
distractors: The size of the finished work measured in centimetres in height and in width
The style or movement to which a particular artist's work is generally assigned
The surface onto which paint is applied, such as canvas, board or plaster
items.note: Medium is the material; support is the surface.
items.example: Bronze is an unforgiving medium.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Motif'.
items.correct: Recurring element
distractors: Overall subject
Personal style
Underlying message
items.note: A motif is a repeated image or pattern within or across works.
items.example: The wave motif recurs throughout the series.

items.question: What does provenance record?
items.correct: The documented history of who has owned a work of art from its creation to the present
distractors: The scientific tests carried out to establish whether a work is genuine or a forgery
The set of documents that must accompany a work when it is exported abroad
The price a work has achieved each time it has been offered for sale at public auction
items.note: Provenance is the ownership chain, key to authenticity and title.
items.example: Gaps in the provenance raised concerns about looting.

items.question: What does restoration involve?
items.correct: Repairing and cleaning a work that has been damaged, bringing it close to its original state
distractors: Preventing further deterioration by controlling light, temperature and humidity around a work
Making an exact copy of a work so that the fragile original need not be put on display
Recording a work in detail with photographs so that its condition can be compared later
items.note: Restoration repairs; conservation prevents further damage.
items.example: The restoration removed centuries of darkened varnish.

items.question: Identify the best B2 meaning of 'Aesthetic'.
items.correct: Concerned with beauty
distractors: Concerned with meaning
Concerned with usefulness
Concerned with cost
items.note: Aesthetic relates to beauty and the appreciation of it.
items.example: The building's aesthetic qualities outweigh its practical faults.

items.question: What does 'contemporary art' mean?
items.correct: Art that is being made by living artists in the present day rather than the past
distractors: Art made in a style that deliberately breaks with the traditions of the recent past
Art produced during the twentieth century from roughly 1900 until the year 2000
Art that uses new technologies such as video, digital media and computer software
items.note: Contemporary means of the present; modern refers to a historical period.
items.example: The gallery specialises in contemporary Thai art.

items.question: Identify the best B1/B2 synonym for 'Depict'.
items.correct: Represent
distractors: Describe
Imagine
Photograph
items.note: To depict is to show something in a picture or sculpture.
items.example: The frieze depicts a procession of horsemen.

items.question: What is an engraving?
items.correct: A print taken from lines that have been cut directly into a plate of metal with a tool
distractors: A picture formed by acid biting into a metal plate through a protective waxy coating
An image created by drawing on stone with a greasy crayon before printing from it
An image transferred to paper by pressing it against an inked screen through a stencil
items.note: Engraving cuts directly; etching uses acid.
items.example: The engraving reproduces a lost painting.

items.question: Identify the best antonym for 'Foreground'.
items.correct: Background
distractors: Frame
Centre
Vanishing point
items.note: The foreground is the nearest part of the depicted space.
items.example: Two figures occupy the foreground.

items.question: What does genre mean in art history?
items.correct: A recognised category of subject matter, such as portraiture, landscape or still life
distractors: A distinctive manner of working shared by a group of artists during one particular period
The technique and materials characteristic of the workshop in which an artist was trained
The intended audience for whom a particular work of art was originally created
items.note: Genre classifies subject; style classifies manner.
items.example: Still life was long considered a minor genre.

items.question: What is an installation?
items.correct: A work conceived for a particular space, which the viewer enters and experiences whole
distractors: A temporary exhibition of works borrowed from several different museums and collections
A large sculpture placed permanently outdoors in a public square or a park setting
The process of hanging and lighting works in a gallery before an exhibition opens
items.note: Installation art is spatial and often site-specific.
items.example: Her installation fills the entire turbine hall.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Juxtapose'.
items.correct: Place side by side
distractors: Blend together
Layer one over another
Repeat at intervals
items.note: Juxtaposition sets two things next to each other for contrast.
items.example: The show juxtaposes medieval icons with digital work.

items.question: What is a mural?
items.correct: A painting executed directly onto the wall or the ceiling of a building itself
distractors: A very large canvas that has been designed to cover most of the wall of a room
A decorative pattern applied to a ceiling in a religious or a public building
A picture assembled from small coloured tiles set into mortar on a flat surface
items.note: A mural is painted onto the architecture itself.
items.example: The mural covers the entire south wall of the school.

items.question: What does Realism as a movement emphasise?
items.correct: Showing ordinary people and the details of everyday life honestly and without idealising
distractors: Reproducing surfaces so precisely that the painting resembles a high-quality photograph
Painting outdoors in order to capture the fleeting effects of natural light on a subject
Choosing heroic historical subjects and treating them with dignity and careful accuracy
items.note: Realism is about honest, unidealised subject matter.
items.example: Realism rejected the grand themes of academic painting.

items.question: Who is a patron in the art world?
items.correct: A person or body that provides an artist or institution with financial support over time
distractors: Someone who buys works of art regularly in order to build a personal collection
Someone who advises wealthy buyers on which works are worth acquiring and at what price
Someone who visits galleries and exhibitions frequently and supports them by paying entry
items.note: A patron funds creation; a collector merely purchases the results.
items.example: The Medici were the most famous patrons of their age.

items.question: What is a portrait?
items.correct: A work of art that represents one particular identifiable person, usually the face
distractors: A picture of a human figure used to study anatomy and the proportions of the body
A painting showing a group of people engaged in an everyday activity in their home
An image of a person produced from memory rather than from a live sitting session
items.note: A portrait represents an identifiable individual.
items.example: The portrait hangs in the entrance hall.

items.question: Identify the best B2 synonym for 'Render' in 'rendered in charcoal'.
items.correct: Execute
distractors: Imagine
Display
Copy
items.note: To render is to produce or represent something in a given medium.
items.example: The drapery is rendered with extraordinary delicacy.

items.question: What is a relief in sculpture?
items.correct: A carved design that projects from a flat background to which it remains attached
distractors: A sculpture that can be viewed from every side and stands freely away from any wall
A cast made by pouring molten metal into a mould taken from an original clay model
A pattern painted onto a flat wall to give the illusion of projecting from it
items.note: Relief projects from a background it remains attached to.
items.example: The temple relief shows a royal procession.

items.question: What does symbolism in a painting involve?
items.correct: The use of objects or images to stand for ideas or qualities beyond their literal sense
distractors: Including small details that help the viewer identify when and where the scene is set
Repeating a particular shape or colour throughout the work to unify the composition
Depicting religious figures according to conventions that viewers would readily recognise
items.note: A symbol carries meaning beyond its literal identity.
items.example: The skull is conventional symbolism for mortality.

items.question: What does texture refer to in a work of art?
items.correct: The surface quality of a work of art, whether it is really present or only suggested
distractors: The thickness of the paint layer measured from the surface of the canvas underneath
The way in which colours have been mixed together before being applied to the surface
The pattern created by the repetition of a small motif across the whole of a surface
items.note: Texture can be actual (impasto) or implied (painted illusion).
items.example: The impasto gives the sky a ridged texture.

items.question: Identify the best B2 antonym for 'Vibrant' describing colour.
items.correct: Muted
distractors: Dark
Glossy
Warm
items.note: Vibrant colours are bright and intense; muted ones are subdued.
items.example: The vibrant reds dominate the upper half.

items.question: Identify the best B2 meaning of 'Avant-garde'.
items.correct: Experimental and ahead of its time
distractors: Widely popular with a mainstream audience
Expensive and highly sought after
Trained in the academic tradition
items.note: The avant-garde pushes beyond accepted conventions.
items.example: The gallery championed avant-garde photography.
